title: Aggregates and window functions in Fabric: traps for SQL Server habits
summary: Fabric Warehouse and the Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint support STRING_AGG with WITHIN GROUP, APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT, APPROX_PERCENTILE_CONT/DISC, PERCENTILE_CONT/DISC, GROUPING/GROUPING_ID with ROLLUP/CUBE/GROUPING SETS, ANY_VALUE, LAG/LEAD/FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE and CHECKSUM_AGG. The traps are about syntax and types. Unlike SQL Server, PERCENTILE_CONT also compiles as a plain grouped aggregate without OVER. The APPROX_ percentile variants are plain aggregates. Some functions return float, tinyint or int when you might expect another type. STRING_AGG does not take DISTINCT. RANGE frames only take UNBOUNDED and CURRENT ROW. LAST_VALUE has a default frame that silently returns the current row. Confidence is high only where the behaviour is well established. Low-confidence claims, including several expected error numbers, still need to be checked by their probes.

claims.statement: In Fabric, PERCENTILE_CONT compiles as a plain grouped aggregate without an OVER clause and returns float. This differs from SQL Server, where OVER is mandatory, so code written this way is not portable back to SQL Server.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY v) AS p FROM (VALUES (1),(2),(3)) AS t(v);
claims.sql_server: Differs from SQL Server: there PERCENTILE_CONT requires an OVER clause and this query fails to compile.
claims.alternative: For code that must also run on SQL Server, use PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY v) OVER (PARTITION BY ...) with SELECT DISTINCT.

claims.statement: PERCENTILE_CONT returns float even when the ordered column is decimal. Cast the result back if exact decimal output matters.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT DISTINCT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY v) OVER () AS p FROM (VALUES (CAST(1.50 AS decimal(10,2))),(CAST(2.50 AS decimal(10,2)))) AS t(v);
claims.sql_server: Same in SQL Server: PERCENTILE_CONT returns float.
claims.alternative: CAST(PERCENTILE_CONT(...) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY v) OVER (...) AS decimal(p,s))

claims.statement: APPROX_PERCENTILE_CONT and APPROX_PERCENTILE_DISC are plain aggregates. They take WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...) and work with GROUP BY, with no OVER clause.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT APPROX_PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY v) AS p FROM (VALUES (1.0E0),(2.0E0),(3.0E0)) AS t(v);

claims.statement: Adding OVER to APPROX_PERCENTILE_CONT, as you would for PERCENTILE_CONT, is rejected.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT APPROX_PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY v) OVER () AS p FROM (VALUES (1.0E0),(2.0E0)) AS t(v);
claims.alternative: Drop OVER and use GROUP BY. Or switch to PERCENTILE_CONT ... OVER (...) for a per-row value.

claims.statement: APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT returns bigint, not int. Size target columns and variables accordingly.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(v) AS c FROM (VALUES ('a'),('b'),('a')) AS t(v);

claims.statement: STRING_AGG with WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...) compiles. On non-max varchar input the result is varchar(8000), so long lists can overflow. Cast the input to varchar(max) to lift the limit.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT STRING_AGG(v, ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY v) AS s FROM (VALUES ('b'),('a')) AS t(v);
claims.sql_server: In SQL Server, non-max varchar input also yields varchar(8000), and the aggregate fails at run time if the result exceeds 8000 bytes.
claims.alternative: STRING_AGG(CAST(v AS varchar(max)), ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY v)

claims.statement: STRING_AGG does not accept DISTINCT. Writing STRING_AGG(DISTINCT v, ',') fails to compile.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT STRING_AGG(DISTINCT v, ',') AS s FROM (VALUES ('a'),('a'),('b')) AS t(v);
claims.sql_server: Same in SQL Server: DISTINCT is not allowed in STRING_AGG.
claims.alternative: Remove duplicates first: SELECT STRING_AGG(v, ',') FROM (SELECT DISTINCT v FROM ...) AS d.

claims.statement: ANY_VALUE is available as an aggregate. It returns an arbitrary value from the group, so use it only when all values in the group are known to be equal.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT k, ANY_VALUE(v) AS v FROM (VALUES (1,10),(1,10),(2,20)) AS t(k,v) GROUP BY k;
claims.alternative: MIN(v) or MAX(v) when a deterministic choice is needed.

claims.statement: LAG and LEAD accept IGNORE NULLS between the call and OVER. This is the way to carry the last non-null value forward.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT LAG(v) IGNORE NULLS OVER (ORDER BY k) AS prev_v FROM (VALUES (1,5),(2,CAST(NULL AS int)),(3,7)) AS t(k,v);
claims.alternative: LAST_VALUE(v) IGNORE NULLS OVER (ORDER BY k ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING)

claims.statement: With ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the frame defaults to RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. LAST_VALUE then silently returns the current row's value. Always spell out the frame.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT LAST_VALUE(v) OVER (ORDER BY k ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_v FROM (VALUES (1,5),(2,6),(3,7)) AS t(k,v);
claims.sql_server: Same default frame in SQL Server.
claims.alternative: FIRST_VALUE(v) OVER (ORDER BY k DESC) gives the last value without a frame clause.

claims.statement: RANGE frames only accept UNBOUNDED PRECEDING/FOLLOWING and CURRENT ROW. A numeric offset such as RANGE BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is rejected.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY k RANGE BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS s FROM (VALUES (1,5),(2,6)) AS t(k,v);
claims.alternative: Use ROWS BETWEEN n PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, or a self-join on the value range.

claims.statement: GROUPING returns tinyint and GROUPING_ID returns int. Both work with ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS to tell subtotal rows from real NULL keys.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT GROUPING(k) AS g, GROUPING_ID(k) AS gid, SUM(v) AS s FROM (VALUES ('a',1),('b',2)) AS t(k,v) GROUP BY ROLLUP(k);

claims.statement: CHECKSUM_AGG only takes integer input. Passing a string column fails, so hash the row first.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT CHECKSUM_AGG(v) AS c FROM (VALUES ('a'),('b')) AS t(v);
claims.sql_server: Same in SQL Server: CHECKSUM_AGG requires an integer expression.

claims.statement: AVG over an int column returns int and truncates silently: the average of 1 and 2 is 1. Cast the input to decimal or float first.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT AVG(v) AS a FROM (VALUES (1),(2)) AS t(v);
